flatmates.title: New flatmates
flatmates.text:
Mia: Hi! You're the new flatmate, aren't you? I'm Mia.
Leo: Yes, I'm Leo. Nice to meet you. I'm moving in today, as you can see!
Mia: Do you need any help with those boxes?

Mia: So, where do you come from, Leo?

Mia: I'm from Cork, in Ireland. What do you do?
Leo: I'm a designer. I work for a small company near the station. And you?
Mia: I'm a nurse, but I'm not working this week. I'm studying for an exam.
Leo: How long do you usually work? Nurses work long hours, don't they?

profile.title: Meet the team: Hana
profile.text:
This month we introduce Hana, who works in our customer service team.

Hana is in her thirties. She is medium height and slim, with short curly hair. People say she looks like her mother, but she is more like her father: quiet, patient and very reliable. “I'm quite shy with strangers,” she says, “but I'm talkative with friends.”

Hana comes from a small town in the north. She lives in a flat near the river and shares it with her sister. They get on well, although they don't have much in common: Hana is tidy and her sister is messy!

Hana usually starts work at eight. She answers about forty e-mails a day and talks to customers on the phone. She rarely eats lunch at her desk: she prefers to go for a walk. Twice a week she trains with a running club, and she occasionally takes part in races.

At the moment Hana is learning Spanish. She is saving money for a long holiday in South America, so she is not eating out much these days. “I don't own a car and I hardly ever buy clothes,” she laughs. “However, I spend too much on books.”

email.text:
Dear Mr and Mrs Reid,

My name is Pavel and I am going to stay with you in July. I would like to tell you something about myself.

I am twenty-four and I come from Brno. I work in a bank, but at the moment I am also doing an evening course in English, because I need it for my job. I am quite a quiet person, although I like meeting new people.

In my free time I play the piano and I go cycling every other day. I am keen on cooking too, so I am happy to help in the kitchen. I do not smoke and I am tidy.

I have two questions. How far is your house from the school? And what kind of food do you usually eat? I eat everything, but I do not like very spicy food.

I am looking forward to meeting you both.

Best wishes,
Pavel

weekend.title: How was your weekend?
weekend.text:
Nina: Hi, Omar! How was your weekend?
Omar: It was great, thanks. I went to the coast with my cousins.
Nina: Lucky you! Did you drive there?
Omar: No, we didn't. We took the train. It was only an hour and a half.
Nina: What did you do there?
Omar: We walked along the beach, ate fish and chips and visited a small museum. What about you? Were you at home?
Nina: No, I wasn't. I was at my sister's. She moved to a new flat last week, so I helped her.
Omar: Did you carry all the boxes?
Nina: I carried about thirty! I didn't sleep well on Saturday because my back hurt.
Omar: Poor you. Did she say thank you?
Nina: She did. She cooked a lovely dinner and gave me a plant for my kitchen.
Omar: That was kind of her. When did you get back?

holiday.title: The worst journey — and the best holiday
holiday.text:
Last summer my friend Rosa and I decided to go to a small village on the coast of Croatia. We booked the flights in March and planned everything very carefully. But the journey didn't go as we planned!

First, we arrived at the airport early, at six in the morning. Then we heard the bad news: there was a storm, and our flight had a delay of five hours. We sat in a café, drank too much coffee and read all our magazines.

After that, we finally got on the plane. The flight was fine, but when we landed, my suitcase wasn't there. I waited for an hour, but it didn't come. Unfortunately, all my summer clothes were in it.

Later, we took a bus to the village. It was dark when we arrived, and we couldn't find the house. Suddenly a dog began to bark, and an old woman came out of a door. Luckily, she knew the owner of our house, and she walked there with us.

In the end, everything was fine. My suitcase arrived two days later. We swam every morning, ate wonderful food and met some very friendly people. It was the worst journey of my life — and the best holiday.

life.title: My grandmother's story
life.text:
My grandmother, Elena, was born in 1941 in a small village in the mountains. She had four brothers and she was the only girl. Her childhood wasn't easy: the family didn't have much money, and the children walked five kilometres to school.

Elena loved books. At the age of seventeen she left the village and moved to the city. She worked in a shop during the day and studied in the evening. Four years later she graduated and became a teacher of mathematics.

In the 1960s she met my grandfather at a dance. He was a bus driver, and he couldn't dance at all! They got married a year later and had two children: my mother and my uncle.

My grandmother taught at the same school for thirty-five years. She knew every family in the town. She retired in 1999, but she didn't stop working: she began to teach children from poor families at home, and she never took any money for it.

She died three years ago, at the age of eighty. I still have her old maths books. When I open them, I remember her voice: “Don't be afraid of mistakes. Be afraid of doing nothing.”

powercut.title: The night the lights went out
powercut.text:
One evening last winter I was at home alone. It was snowing outside and the wind was blowing hard. I was sitting on the sofa and reading a detective story, and my cat was sleeping next to me.

Suddenly, while I was reading the most frightening page, all the lights went out. At first I thought it was just my flat, but when I looked out of the window, the whole street was dark. It was a power cut.

I couldn't find my torch, so I lit a candle. As I was walking to the kitchen, I heard a noise upstairs. Somebody was moving a chair! But I live on the top floor, and there is nothing above my flat — only the roof.

I was really frightened. I stood still and listened. The noise stopped. Then, a few minutes later, somebody knocked at my door. I didn't open it. “Who is it?” I whispered.

“It's Mr Novak from next door,” a voice said. “I was fixing my aerial on the roof when the lights went out. I couldn't see anything, and I dropped my keys. Have you got a torch?”

I was so relieved that I began to laugh. We found the torch together — it was in the fridge. Don't ask me why.

accident.title: What did you see?
accident.text:
Police officer: Good morning. You saw the accident, didn't you? Can you tell me what happened?
Witness: Yes, of course. I was waiting at the bus stop on the corner.
Police officer: What time was that?
Witness: About ten past eight. It was raining, so I was standing under the roof of the shop.
Police officer: What was the cyclist doing?
Witness: He was riding along the road, quite fast. He was wearing a dark jacket, and he wasn't using any lights.
Police officer: And the car?
Witness: The car was coming out of the car park. The driver was looking to the right, I think. She didn't see the cyclist.
Police officer: What happened next?
Witness: The cyclist tried to stop, but the road was wet, and he slipped. He hit the side of the car and fell on the pavement.
Police officer: Was he badly hurt?
Witness: He cut his hand and hurt his knee, but he could stand up. The driver got out at once and called an ambulance.
Police officer: Were the traffic lights working?
Witness: Yes, they were. They were green for the cyclist.
Police officer: Thank you. That's very helpful.

wedding.title: The speech
wedding.text:
My brother got married last June, and he asked me to give a speech at the wedding. I was excited, but also very worried, because I am not a confident speaker.

On the day, everything was going well. The sun was shining, the guests were chatting and laughing, and a small band was playing in the garden. I was sitting next to my aunt, and I was reading my speech again and again.

Then my moment came. As I was walking to the front, I realised that the paper in my hand was not my speech. It was my shopping list! By the time I noticed, everybody was looking at me. I couldn't go back.

At first I was so embarrassed that I couldn't say a word. Then I decided to tell the truth. “I wrote a beautiful speech,” I said, “but it is at home, on my fridge. Here I have only this: milk, eggs, washing powder.”

To my surprise, everybody began to laugh, and my brother laughed more than anybody. So I spoke without notes — about our childhood, about the day he met his wife, about how happy he looked. It turned out to be the best speech of my life.

travel.title: Have you ever…?
travel.text:
Nadia: Tom, have you ever been to Morocco?
Tom: No, I haven't. I've never been to Africa. Why?
Nadia: I'm planning a holiday. I've been to Spain and Portugal, but I want to see something different.
Tom: My sister has been to Morocco twice. She loved it.
Nadia: Really? What did she do there?
Tom: The first time she stayed in Marrakesh. The second time, two years ago, she went to the desert and rode a camel.
Nadia: I've never ridden a camel. Have you?
Tom: No, but I've ridden a horse. Once. I fell off after five minutes.
Nadia: Poor you! Have you ever tried Moroccan food?
Tom: Yes, I have. There's a good Moroccan restaurant near the station. I ate there last month.
Nadia: Was it good?
Tom: It was fantastic. I had lamb with apricots. I've never eaten anything like it.
Nadia: Then let's go there on Friday. You can tell me more about your sister's trips.
Tom: Good idea. I'll ask her for some photos.

news.title: An e-mail with news
news.text:
Hi Sofia,

How are things? I'm sorry I haven't written lately — a lot has happened!

Guess what: I've moved house. Three weeks ago I left my little room in the centre, and now I live in a flat near the river. It's bigger and quieter, and I've already met two of my neighbours. I haven't bought a sofa yet, so my guests sit on the floor.

I've got more news. I've passed my driving test! I failed it in March, but I took it again last Friday and passed. I haven't driven alone yet — I'm still a bit frightened.

Unfortunately, I've lost my phone, so I've got a new number. I left the old one on a train last week. Luckily, all my photos were on my laptop.

By the way, have you heard from Daniel? He has gone to Canada for six months. He sent me a postcard from Toronto.

Anyway, what about you? Have you finished your course yet? Write soon and tell me everything.

I'm looking forward to hearing from you.

Best wishes,
Alma

Good evening. Here is the weather forecast for the weekend.

Tomorrow, Saturday, will start cold and clear, with temperatures of about two degrees in the morning. It will be sunny until lunchtime, but clouds will arrive from the west in the afternoon, and there might be a few showers in the evening.

Sunday will be very different. It will be wet and windy all day, with heavy rain in the north. In the mountains the rain may turn to snow. There might be a storm on the coast on Sunday night, so please be careful if you are driving.

The good news is that it will be mild: the temperature won't fall below eight degrees.

Next week will probably be dry, but it is too early to be sure.

So — if you are planning a walk, go tomorrow morning. And on Sunday, don't forget your umbrella. You'll definitely need it.

planet.title: Our planet
planet.text:
Here are some facts about our planet and its neighbours. How many do you know?

The highest mountain on Earth is Mount Everest, in the Himalayas. The largest and deepest ocean is the Pacific: it is bigger than all the land on Earth together.

The largest country in the world is Russia, and the smallest is Vatican City, which is inside the city of Rome.

The coldest continent is Antarctica. It is also the windiest and the driest — yes, drier than the deserts of Africa, because it almost never rains or snows there.

The largest animal on Earth is the blue whale. The fastest animal on land is the cheetah, but it is not the fastest animal of all: some birds are faster when they fly down from the sky.

And in space? The biggest planet near our Sun is Jupiter. The smallest is Mercury, which is also the closest to the Sun. But Mercury is not the hottest planet. Venus is further from the Sun, and it is even hotter.

review.title: Two cafés in my street
review.text:
There are two cafés in my street, and people often ask me which one is better. Here is my opinion.

The Corner Cup is the older one. It is small and dark, but the atmosphere is lovely, and the staff are the friendliest in town — they know my name and my order. The coffee is excellent. On the other hand, it is always crowded, the chairs are not very comfortable, and it is too noisy to work there.

Bean House opened last year. It is much more modern and more spacious, and it has the fastest wi-fi in the neighbourhood. It is quiet enough for work, and the cakes are better than at the Corner Cup. However, the coffee is not as good, and it is more expensive. The service is slower too, and one waiter was quite rude to me.

Overall, the Corner Cup is better value for money. In my opinion, it is the best place for a quick coffee with a friend. But if you need to work for a few hours, Bean House is worth the higher price. I recommend both — for different days.

Manager: Welcome to the team, Kofi. Let me tell you a few rules.

Kofi: Can I take a break in the morning?
Manager: Yes, you can have a fifteen-minute break at ten. Lunch is at one.
Kofi: Do we have to work overtime?
Manager: Not usually. Last month we had to stay late twice because two colleagues were ill, but that doesn't happen often.
Kofi: Are we allowed to use our phones?
Manager: You can use them in the staff room, but you mustn't use them in the shop. And you mustn't give your password to anybody — not even to me.

Elif: Yes, please. I've got a sore throat and a bad cough, and I feel very tired.
Chemist: Oh dear. How long have you had the cough?
Elif: It started three days ago.
Chemist: Have you got a temperature?
Elif: I don't think so. But I've got a headache.
Chemist: It sounds like a cold. You should drink a lot of warm tea with honey, and you should rest. You shouldn't go to work today.
Elif: I have to go — we've got a deadline.
Chemist: Then you should at least go home early. Take these tablets for your throat: one every four hours. You mustn't take more than six a day.
Elif: Do I need a prescription?
Chemist: No, you don't have to have a prescription for these.
Elif: Should I see a doctor?
Chemist: Not yet. But if you don't feel better in three days, or if you get a temperature, you should see one.
Elif: Thank you. How much is that?

village.title: A weekend in the middle of nowhere
village.text:
Last month I needed a rest, so I rented a small house in a village in the mountains. My friends said, “There's nothing to do there!” They were right — and it was wonderful.

When I arrived on Friday evening, I didn't see anybody in the street. Everything was closed. There was nowhere to buy food, and I had nothing in my bag except an apple. Luckily, somebody knocked at my door: it was the woman from the house next door, with a bowl of hot soup. “Everybody here knows you've arrived,” she said. “We've got only forty people, so new faces are big news.”

On Saturday I walked everywhere. I didn't meet anyone on the paths — only a few sheep. In the afternoon I looked for somewhere to have coffee. There wasn't a café anywhere, but an old man invited me into his garden and gave me tea and something sweet made with honey.

On Sunday nobody was in a hurry, and I wasn't either. I read, I slept, and I didn't check my phone — there was no signal anywhere.

I came home with nothing in my bag, but I felt that I had everything I needed.

recipe.title: Easy vegetable soup
recipe.text:
This soup is cheap, healthy and very easy. It takes about forty minutes and makes four portions.

Ingredients: two onions, three carrots, two potatoes, a tin of tomatoes, a litre of water, a little oil, a pinch of salt and some pepper. You can also add a few mushrooms or anything else you have in the fridge.

First, peel the onions, the carrots and the potatoes, and chop them into small pieces.

Next, heat a little oil in a large saucepan. Add the onions and fry them for five minutes. Stir them all the time — they mustn't burn.

Then add the carrots and the potatoes and fry everything for a few more minutes.

After that, pour in the water and add the tomatoes, the salt and the pepper. Boil the soup, then turn the heat down and cook it gently for twenty-five minutes, until the vegetables are soft.

Finally, taste the soup. If there isn't enough salt, add a little more. Serve it hot, with a slice of bread and a spoonful of cream.

The soup is even better the next day, so make plenty!

ambitions.text:
We asked three people in our town about their plans and their free time.

Sandra, 34, nurse. “I enjoy helping people, but I can't stand working at night. I've decided to study again: I hope to become a children's doctor. I need to pass two exams first. I spend all my free time reading — I've even given up watching TV. My family has promised to help with the children.”

Marcus, 19, student. “I'm keen on cooking, and my dream is to open a small café. I'm learning to bake bread — I keep burning it, but I refuse to give up. My father suggested working in a restaurant first, and I've agreed to try it this summer. I don't mind washing dishes if I can watch the cooks.”

Grace, 67, retired teacher. “I've finished working, but I can't sit at home without doing anything. I'm interested in learning languages, and I would like to visit Japan next year. I'm not very good at remembering new words, so I practise every morning instead of reading the news. I expect to speak badly — but I'm not afraid of making mistakes.”

visit.title: How to find me
visit.text:
Hi Tomas,

I'm so glad you're coming on Friday! Here are the directions to my flat.

When you arrive at the central station, don't take a taxi — it's expensive, and the traffic is terrible. Take tram number 4 instead. The stop is opposite the main exit. You need to buy a ticket before you get on: there's a machine at the stop.

Get off at Market Square — it takes about fifteen minutes. If you see a big blue bridge, you've gone too far; in that case, get off and walk back.

From Market Square it's five minutes on foot. Go straight ahead until you see a bakery with a green door. My building is next to it, number 18. You can't miss it. The entrance is at the side. I'm on the third floor.

Text me as soon as your train leaves, and I'll put the soup on. If your train is delayed, don't worry — I won't go to bed until you get here. And if I don't answer the door, give me a ring: the bell doesn't always work.

I suggest bringing a warm jacket. I'm planning to show you the old town on Saturday, and we'll go hiking on Sunday unless it rains.

Have a safe journey!
Mila

friends.title: Twenty years of friendship
friends.text:
This month Nina and I celebrate an anniversary: we have been friends for twenty years.

We met at primary school, when we were seven. She sat next to me on the first day and gave me half of her sandwich. We have been best friends ever since.

We don't have much in common. Nina has always been keen on sport; I have never run for a bus in my life. She has lived in the same town all her life, and she has worked at the local hospital since 2019. I have moved five times, and I have had four different jobs.

For three years we lived in different countries. Many friends lose touch when that happens, but we stayed in touch: we talked every Sunday evening.

Nina has been married for six years, and she has had her dog, Pepper, since her wedding day — he was a present from her husband. I have known her husband for ages too: he was in our class.

People sometimes ask how we have managed to get on so well for so long. I think the answer is simple. We have never tried to change each other — and she still shares her sandwiches.

tea.title: From the leaf to your cup
tea.text:
Tea is the most popular drink in the world after water. But how does it get to your cup?

Tea is grown in warm, wet places. A lot of it is produced in China, India, Kenya and Sri Lanka. The tea plant is kept short, about a metre high, so that the leaves can be picked easily.

Only the young leaves at the top are used. On many farms they are still picked by hand, because machines also take the old leaves.

After that, the leaves are taken to a factory. For black tea, they are left in the air for a few hours until they turn dark, and then they are dried. For green tea, the leaves are heated quickly, so they stay green. Both kinds are made from the same plant!

Next, the tea is packed into large bags and exported. It is sent by ship to countries all over the world. There it is put into small packets or tea bags and delivered to shops.

Finally, it is bought, taken home — and often forgotten at the back of a cupboard. Tea should be kept in a dry, dark place, and it is best when it is drunk within a year.

facts.title: Who, when, where?
facts.text:
How much do you know about famous buildings, pictures and discoveries?

The Eiffel Tower was built for a world exhibition in Paris in 1889. It is named after Gustave Eiffel, whose company built it. At first it was planned to stand for only twenty years.

The Taj Mahal in India was built in the seventeenth century. It was built by the emperor Shah Jahan in memory of his wife.

The Mona Lisa was painted by Leonardo da Vinci at the beginning of the sixteenth century. In 1911 it was stolen from the Louvre museum in Paris, and it was found two years later.

Penicillin was discovered by the scientist Alexander Fleming in 1928 — by accident. Since then, millions of lives have been saved by this medicine.

The first modern Olympic Games were held in Athens in 1896.

The first person was sent into space in 1961. His name was Yuri Gagarin, and his flight took less than two hours.

The World Wide Web was invented by Tim Berners-Lee in 1989. Today it is used by billions of people — and this lesson was brought to you by it.
